# Moving the simplex comparison point: an exact orbit floor and its limit

Let `K` be a full-dimensional simplex with centroid zero, let `P` be
finite, and let the actual compatible fibers be
`K_p=c_p+r_p K`, with all `r_p>0`. Fix a vertex `v0` of `K`, put
`T=K-v0`, and use the one common-vertex source with fibers `r_p T`.
For an anchor `j` and `Z in K` define

    D_j(Z) = depth_star(j, r_j(Z-v0)).

Let `G` be the finite group of all vertex permutations of the centered
simplex, represented as linear maps. Then the following movable-point
comparison holds:

    depth_actual(j,c_j+r_j Z) >= min_(A in G) D_j(A Z).       (1)

However its optimized right side is exactly the old centroid bound:

    max_(Z in K) min_(A in G) D_j(A Z) = D_j(0).             (2)

Thus moving the candidate cannot improve this particular orbit-minimum
certificate. This does not exclude a stronger comparison that retains
the coupling between each normal and its corresponding orbit point.

## 1. The candidate displacement under an actual cap comparison

For a nonzero continuous normal `u`, choose a minimizing vertex `v`
of `K`, and put `a=-u.v>0`. The support-minorant theorem in
`candidate 24467ade6f021ae8`
gives a vector `b` such that

    u.(c_p-c_j) >= a(r_p-r_j)+b.(p-j).

An original cap through `(j,c_j+r_j Z)` has margin

    beta.(p-j)+u.(x-c_j-r_j Z).

At `x=c_p+r_p X`, with `X in K`, this is at least

    (beta+b).(p-j)+a(r_p-r_j)+r_p u.X-r_j u.Z.               (3)

Use the comparison fibers

    L_p=(r_j-r_p)v+r_p K.

Expression (3) is exactly the margin of an ambient cap through
`(j,r_j Z)` on this comparison source. Its parameterization from `K`
has the same Jacobian `r_p^d` as the actual source, so its cap mass
does not exceed the original cap mass, fiber by fiber.

Choose `A in G` with `A v0=v`. The volume-preserving map

    x -> A^(-1)(x-r_j v)

sends every `L_p` to `r_p T`, but now sends the comparison candidate to

    r_j(A^(-1) Z-v0),                              (4)

not to `r_j(Z-v0)` in general. The transformed cap is therefore
bounded below by `D_j(A^(-1) Z)`, which proves (1) for nonvertical
caps. A purely base-normal cap has identical mass in both sources and
contains every continuous point over `j`, so it also satisfies (1).
Containing caps can be moved parallel until they pass through the
candidate. All boundaries and all finite-rank base cases have the
same treatment as in the support-minorant theorem.

The choice of `A` among maps sending `v0` to `v` causes no additional
ambiguity: two such choices differ on the right by a permutation
fixing `v0`. Such a permutation preserves the entire source `r_p T`
and hence preserves its depth. There are at most `d+1` distinct
orbit values needed in (1), one for each vertex designated as the
common vertex. Repeated barycentric coordinates may reduce this count.

## 2. Quasiconcavity makes the floor centroid-limited

Depth on the fixed base fiber is quasiconcave. Indeed, a closed
halfspace containing a convex combination of finitely many points
contains at least one of those points; its mass is therefore at least
the minimum of their depths. This argument needs no attainment or
regularity assertion about the optimizing cap.

The average of `{A Z : A in G}` is zero. In barycentric coordinates,
each of the `d+1` entries appears equally often at every vertex, so
each averaged barycentric coordinate is `1/(d+1)`. Consequently
quasiconcavity gives

    D_j(0) >= min_(A in G) D_j(A Z)               for every Z in K.

At `Z=0` all orbit points agree, proving equality (2). The maximum
in (2) is attained without needing continuity, because the explicit
candidate `Z=0` achieves the upper bound.

## 3. Exact failure of the orbit certificate despite a useful moved point

Take the actual planar body with integer interval fibers

    I_0=[0,2], I_1=[0,6], I_2=[0,10], I_3=[0,3].

Its radius sequence is concave, with successive differences `4,4,-7`,
so it is a common-vertex simplex chain. Its mixed mass is `21`.
The following closed caps through the four own midpoints have masses
`1,5,5,3/2`, respectively:

    x >= 11 z+1;
    x >= 11(z-1)+3;
    x >= 9-2z;
    x >= -11(z-3)+3/2.

Thus at every anchor the optimized orbit floor in (2) is at most
`5 < 21/4`. This is the existing own-midpoint counterexample, now
applied to the exact moved-point certificate rather than claimed as
a new body counterexample.

In contrast the actual moved point `(2,3)` has depth at least `6`.
The source contains the centrally symmetric retained measure with
fibers `[3,6]` at base 1, `[0,6]` at base 2, and `[0,3]` at base 3.
Its mass is `12`, and reflection about `(2,3)` exchanges its endpoint
fibers and preserves its middle fiber. Any closed halfspace containing
the center captures at least half its mass. Hence the orbit-floor loss
is real even in a body with an explicitly sufficient moved point.

The exact cap and retention checks are in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_movable_simplex_orbit_floor.py`. The general identities (1)
and (2) are proved above, independently of that finite example.
